faq.a: Feet flat, back supported, shoulders relaxed, forearms roughly parallel to the floor, and the screen top at eye height. Your wrists should float over the keyboard rather than resting heavily on the desk, which keeps your fingers quick and pain-free.

p: A touch typing test measures how fast and how accurately you type without looking at the keys. Touch typing means all ten fingers work from the home row, and your eyes stay on the screen the whole time. This free test runs for 60 seconds, scores your words per minute (WPM) and accuracy live, and highlights every error so you can see exactly which keys still trip you up. Because the practice sentences are taken from real touch typing lessons, taking the test is itself a lesson.

seo.h2: Why take a touch typing test every day
p: Muscle memory is built by frequency, not by marathon sessions. A daily 60 second touch typing test is enough to keep the home row fresh and to expose the two or three keys that always slow you down. Track your WPM across a week and you will see the pattern: accuracy climbs first, and speed follows a few days behind. When your accuracy passes 98 percent, you know the keyboard has finally moved into your fingers.

seo.h2: How to use this touch typing practice
p: Start by resting your index fingers on the small bumps on F and J, with the other fingers curling onto the home row beside them. Type the sentence on screen without glancing down; if you must look, look only after the line is finished. Keep your wrists floating and your shoulders down. After the test, read the error report: those keys, not your fastest ones, are your next practice targets.

faq.q: What is a touch typing test?
faq.a: A touch typing test measures your typing speed and accuracy while you type without looking at the keyboard. This one runs for 60 seconds and reports live WPM, accuracy, and a per-key error summary.

faq.q: Is this touch typing test free?
faq.a: Yes, it is completely free. There is no sign up, no account, and no paywall, and your results are stored only in your own browser.

faq.q: How fast is good touch typing?
faq.a: A comfortable touch typing speed is 40 to 60 WPM, and 70 to 90 WPM is considered fast. Above 100 WPM is competitive territory. Accuracy matters first: most people reach their best speed only after their accuracy passes 97 to 98 percent.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn touch typing?
faq.a: With 10 to 15 minutes of daily practice, most people learn the home row in a week and reach a comfortable 40 to 60 WPM in three to four weeks. The practice sentences on this page come from the same lessons, so the test itself doubles as training.

faq.q: Should I look at the keyboard while testing?
faq.a: No. Cover the keyboard with a piece of paper if you have to, and let the bumps on F and J guide your index fingers. Every glance down is a habit that costs speed later, so train the eyes to stay on the screen.

faq.q: What is the home row?
faq.a: The home row is the middle letter row: A S D F G H J K L ; with the thumbs on the space bar. Every finger owns a small group of keys around the home row, and every finger returns home after each keystroke.

seo.h2: How to race your fastest typing sprint
p: Treat the first sentence like a warm up, not a launch: start at 80 percent of your top speed and build into the race. Keep your eyes on the text two or three words ahead of your fingers, so your hands never stall mid-sentence. Keep your wrists light and your rhythm even, because most typing races are lost in the last ten seconds when fatigue makes fingers sloppy.

seo.h2: Race yourself and track your best WPM
p: Your best time is saved in your own browser, so every race is really against yourself. Try a best-of-three: race once to warm up, once at full speed, and once while aiming for zero corrections. The third race usually produces your best WPM, because chasing accuracy is what unlocks the top speed. Come back daily and the leaderboard of your own history does the rest.

faq.q: What is a typing race?
faq.a: A typing race is a timed typing sprint where you type as fast and as accurately as you can against a countdown. This one gives you 60 seconds and scores your live WPM and accuracy.

faq.q: Is this typing race free?
faq.a: Yes, completely free with no sign up and no account. Just open the page and start racing.

faq.q: How do I get faster in a typing race?
faq.a: Start slightly slower than your top speed and build into the sprint, read a few words ahead of your fingers, and keep your rhythm steady. Most races are decided in the final ten seconds, so finishing cleanly beats starting fast.

faq.q: What is a good WPM for a typing race?
faq.a: Around 50 to 70 WPM is a solid race speed, 80 to 100 WPM is fast, and anything above 100 WPM is competitive. Remember that accuracy multiplies speed: a race with no corrections almost always beats a faster race full of fixes.

faq.q: Can I race against other people?
faq.a: This is a race against the clock and your own saved best score, which keeps it fair and pressure-free. Compare your best WPM with friends by sharing the page; whoever holds the highest clean score wins.

faq.q: How long is the typing race?

p: A good typing tutorial explains why each finger owns certain keys, not just which key to press. This free online typing tutor works the same way: every practice sentence is a lesson in itself, so while you type you absorb the home row, the finger map, and the posture rules at the same time. Sixty seconds of guided practice, live WPM and accuracy feedback, and no sign up, no download, and no cost.

seo.h2: What this typing tutor teaches first
p: The tutorial starts where every typing tutor must: the home row. Your left fingers rest on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ;, with thumbs on the space bar and index fingers on the small bumps of F and J. From there the lessons add the upper and lower rows one at a time, then the shift key, then punctuation. Each step is short on purpose, because a tutorial only works when you can finish it without rushing.

seo.h2: Practice schedule for a typing tutorial
p: Ten to fifteen minutes a day, every day, beats a single long session once a week. Repeat each lesson until it feels boring, then once more: that is the moment muscle memory forms. Close the loop by ending every session on your weakest keys, the ones where your accuracy dips, and those keys will be your strongest within a week.

faq.q: Is this typing tutorial free?
faq.a: Yes. Every lesson is free, with no sign up, no account, and no paywall. You can repeat the tutorial as often as you like, and your results stay in your own browser.

faq.q: Do I need a typing tutor if I already type?
faq.a: If you hunt and peck with two fingers, a typing tutor is the single biggest speed upgrade available. If you already touch type, this tutorial still helps by drilling the keys and rows that drag your accuracy down.

faq.q: How long is the typing tutorial?
faq.a: Each practice round is 60 seconds, and a full beginner pass through the lessons takes about two weeks of 10 to 15 minutes a day. You can move faster or slower; the tutorial is self-paced.

faq.q: What should I learn first in a typing tutorial?
faq.a: The home row, always. Rest your fingers on A S D F J K L ;, find the bumps on F and J with your index fingers, and practice words built only from those keys until you never look down. Everything else is added on top of that foundation.

faq.q: Can a typing tutorial work on a laptop keyboard?
faq.a: Yes. Any standard keyboard works, laptop or desktop. The finger map is identical on QWERTY layouts, and a tutorial that teaches posture and relaxation transfers to any keyboard you own.
